faq.a: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are almost always due to a germline NF2 mutation; sporadic cases are usually unilateral.
faq.q: Why is bilateral disease considered NF2 and not sporadic?

faq.a: Yes, if hearing is preserved and tumors are Koos I‑II, serial MRI and audiometry are the standard approach.
faq.q: Can a child with small tumors be observed safely?

faq.a: When hearing is lost after translabyrinthine surgery, a cochlear implant can restore speech perception, especially in children.
faq.q: What is the role of cochlear implants after tumor removal?

exam: A 9‑year‑old presents with bilateral progressive hearing loss; MRI shows 1.5 cm lesions on both internal auditory canals. What is the next step? — Discuss observation versus early surgery based on Koos stage and hearing status.
How does the Koos classification influence surgical planning for vestibular schwannoma? — Explain each stage and its impact on approach and prognosis.
A child with NF2 develops new facial weakness. Which investigation confirms tumor progression and what finding would you expect? — MRI showing increase in tumor size or brainstem compression.
Why is stereotactic radiosurgery not first‑line in a low‑resource hospital? — Limited equipment, need for precise targeting, and follow‑up imaging constraints.
What bedside tests can suggest vestibular involvement when audiometry is unavailable? — Whisper test, Rinne/Weber, Romberg and gait assessment.
Explain why schwannomatosis is not the diagnosis in a child with bilateral vestibular tumors. — Schwannomatosis lacks bilateral vestibular schwannomas; NF2 is required.
What are the contraindications for using high‑dose steroids peri‑operatively in these patients? — Active infection (e.g., TB, malaria), uncontrolled diabetes, severe hypertension.
A patient develops hydrocephalus secondary to a large Koos IV tumor. What emergency management is required? — Prompt neurosurgical drainage (ventriculostomy) and tumor debulking.
ai.title: Bilateral Vestibular Schwannoma
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are hallmark tumors of NF2, presenting in children with progressive hearing loss, balance problems and facial nerve dysfunction. Early recognition, appropriate imaging and multidisciplinary management are crucial in low‑resource settings.

b: Bilateral tumors → NF2 diagnosis
Unilateral tumor → consider sporadic schwannoma
sections.p: A vestibular schwannoma is a benign tumor of the vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) nerve sheath. When present on both sides, it defines neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). Diagnosis rests on clinical features and MRI of the internal auditory canals.

t.a: MRI brain with gadolinium (or contrast‑enhanced CT if MRI unavailable)
t.b: Confirms tumor size, location and bilateral involvement; absence of MRI → refer for CT or clinical monitoring
Quantifies hearing loss; asymmetric loss suggests tumor side; if audiometer unavailable, bedside whisper test and Rinne/Weber help

b: Koos I: intracanalicular only
Koos II: ≤2 cm, no brainstem compression
Koos III: 2‑3 cm, mild brainstem displacement
Koos IV: >3 cm, significant brainstem/ventricular compression
sections.p: Tumor size and cranial nerve function guide staging. The Koos classification (I‑IV) is used for surgical planning.

b: NF2 autosomal‑dominant mutation (TRAF7, LZTR1 variants also reported)
Rare sporadic bilateral tumors (usually due to radiation exposure)
sections.p: The primary cause is a germline NF2 mutation. In low‑resource regions, co‑existing infections or malnutrition may worsen symptoms but do not cause the tumor.

b: Progressive sensorineural hearing loss
Tinnitus or ear fullness
Unsteady gait, especially in dark
Facial nerve palsy (House‑Brackmann grade II‑IV)
Skin café‑au‑lait spots or other NF2 stigmata
sections.p: Children often present with gradual unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, disequilibrium, and later facial weakness or numbness. Bilateral disease may cause early bilateral hearing loss and balance failure.
Imaging and functional tests confirm diagnosis and guide treatment.

t.a: MRI brain with thin‑slice internal auditory canal protocol
t.b: Result: tumor present → stage; no tumor → consider alternative diagnosis
Result: >40 dB loss → consider intervention; normal → monitor

t.a: Genetic testing for NF2 mutation (if accessible)
t.b: Result: pathogenic variant → counsel relatives; negative → still monitor clinically

b: Sudden worsening of hearing or facial palsy
New onset headache with vomiting (raised intracranial pressure)
Rapidly enlarging tumor on imaging
Hydrocephalus
sections.p: Rapid neurological decline signals urgent intervention.

b: Small Koos I‑II tumors with good hearing: watchful waiting with 6‑month MRI
Progressive hearing loss or Koos III‑IV: microsurgical resection (retrosigmoid or translabyrinthine) – chosen to preserve facial nerve
If surgery not feasible: stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife) – limited availability, consider referral
Adjunctive steroids for peri‑operative edema
Rehabilitation: vestibular physiotherapy, hearing aids or cochlear implant after surgery
sections.p: Treatment balances tumor control, hearing preservation and facial nerve function. Options include observation, radiotherapy and surgery.

b: MRI every 12 months for the first 3 years, then every 2‑3 years
Annual audiometry
Genetic counseling for family members
Vaccinate against meningitis (risk after skull base surgery)
sections.p: Lifelong surveillance is required because new tumors can develop and residual disease can grow.

b: Chronic otitis media with effusion – conductive loss, improves with antibiotics
Labyrinthitis – acute vertigo, usually unilateral
Meningitis – fever, neck stiffness, CSF changes
Schwannomatosis – multiple schwannomas but no bilateral vestibular lesions
sections.p: Other causes of pediatric hearing loss and balance disturbance may mimic bilateral vestibular schwannoma.

b: Normal CT in early disease may miss small intracanalicular tumors – MRI is required
Mild hearing loss on bedside test may underestimate tumor size – formal audiometry needed
sections.p: Certain investigations may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid loss of hearing or facial weakness
New severe headache, vomiting or altered consciousness
Signs of hydrocephalus on exam or imaging
